title: Lily
description:
The wreck is reported to have been dispersed to seabed level. The full character and extent of any archaeological remains is unknown at present time.

Event and Historical Information:
The LILY was a 33 ton wooden trow fitted with an auxiliary engine. The trow was carrying a cargo of coal from Newport to Wick St lawrence which had a small coal quay used by the Weston-Cleveland-Portishead Light Railway Company. Soon after leaving Newport on 25 January 1929, the LILY developed a leak. The vessel was soon so waterlogged that it would not respond to its helm. The master decided to drop anchor in Barry Roads. The Newport pilot cutter NANCY spotted the LILY's plight and came alongside to offer a tow.  However, soon after the tow was taken up, the LILY foundered and the crew were forced to swim for the pilot cutter. The position given for the loss was 51 30 32N, 02 58 54W or bearing 1.93miles 167 degrees from the Usk light. The wreck was marked by a green buoy placed 40yards to the west. Trinity House reported that the wreck to be removed by contract and in November 1929 confirmed that the wreck had been dispersed to seabed level.

Sources include:
Smith, G, 1991, Shipwrecks of the Bristol Channel, pg43-4

title: Lily
description:
This record comprises a documentary reference to a shipping casualty which has been assigned to the maritime named location HARRY FURLONG ROCKS pending more information which may allow a more precise location for the loss to be assigned.

Event and Historical Information:
The LILY was a wooden schooner belonging to the port of Padstow. At time of loss on 19 October 1907, the vessel was on passage from Newferry to Pentewan with a cargo of coal under the command of master . The schooner missed stays when making for Holyhead and struck the West Mouse Rock. The schooner drifted clear, but on the pumps the LILY was found to be making water faster than the pumps could. Attempts were made to beach the schooner at Cemlyn, but it struck rocks on the west side of Mill Bay and sank.  

Sources include:
Lloyds List, 21 October 1907

title: WATER LILY
description:
"Summary: 1917 wreck of English schooner which foundered 8 miles N x E of Pendeen Lighthouse, after being shelled, then stopped and scuttled with charges by UC-51, while bound from Runcorn for Cherbourg. 

She was the fourth of five vessels to be attacked by UC-51 on this day, the first being the MOSS ROSE (906461), then the MARY SEYMOUR (906458) and MARY ORR (1109064). After the attack on the WATER LILY, the JANE WILLIAMSON was sunk later that afternoon (906459). UC-51 would herself be lost in November 1917 but there are variant reports of her last resting place (929128 account of wreck event; 832137 possible remains).

Constructed of wood in 1876, the WATER LILY was a sailing vessel."

title: WATER LILY HOUSE
description: The Water Lily House at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, was built in 1852 to house the giant Amazonian water lilly ('Victoria amazonica'). At the time of its construction the building was the world's largest single span glasshouse with its wrought iron being constructed by Richard Turner, who was also responsible for the Palm House. Unfortunatley, the giant lilly did not thrive in the house and so in 1866 it was converted into an Economic Plant House displaying plants for culinary and medical purposes. During World War II the house suffered bomb damage and was not repaired until 1965. In 1991 the building was completely refurbished and restored to its original role as the Water Lily House and since 1999 'Victoria cruziana' has been grown successfully here.

title: Lily Garth
description:
Lily Garth, a former farmstead that appears to have been in use as a barn for some years. The layout comprises the farm building with outshots attached to the north and off the western gable. The buildings are largely built of coursed sandstone in very rough blocks. There is a very clear thatch line surviving in the eastern gable end, partly showing as a number of quoins at steeply pitched angles. Inside there is a fireplace at in the centre of the east gable wall. This appears to be quite late with a monolith surround. An inward step on the chimney above head height suggests that internally there may previously have been a suspended ceiling. Both changes in quoins and another roofline on the south external elevation suggest that the roof has been raised. This is an interesting building with a clearly complex phasing and would be well worth more detailed survey work. There is a hay sled stored within the roof of the northern outshot.
The main building appears to be relatively stable, but would probably benefit from some minor consolidation works. The outshots are in generally poorer condition and the western outshot has some obvious cracking to the walls. (1)

title: Lily (1496)
description: The Lily, Captain John Owens, master, bound from Liverpool for Ambrazo, southwest Africa, with a general cargo, including 20 puncheons of rum, fire-arms, and 61 tons of gunpowder, was caught off the Calf of Man in the storm of Monday 27th December 1852 after having been driven back up the Irish Sea from Cork in a crippled condition. The sea was mountainous in the southwesterly gale and, despite the efforts of the crew, she was driven ashore at the southeastern point of Kitterland in the Calf Sound at 11.00 a.m. The crew of thirteen men desperately tried to reach the rocks by means of the boats, but huge waves carried off Captain Owens, the cook and two lads, one of whom was the son of the captain. All of them drowned. In addition, one of the masts fell upon the carpenter killing him immediately. The men who died were James Moore, Captain John Owens, John George Owens, Daniel Riordan and John Robinson.As the gale partially abated, hope revived in the hearts of those who remained on shore, that possibly the rest of the eight crew might yet be saved. A boat was brought in a cart from Port St. Mary, a distance of two or three miles, and gallant crews were found to man her, and also the small boat kept at the Sound. Arrived at the Sound, it seemed scarcely possible to launch the boat, from the terrific sea that was everywhere breaking upon the rocks. At length a spot was selected for the trial. She was lowered stern foremost from a considerable height. The attempt was successful, and the crew jumped into her with a long coil of rope made fast to her bow, and held by the multitude on shore. In solemn silence they pushed across the Sound. Hoping against hope, the attempt to land on the Kitterland Rocks was made, with every precaution nautical skill and the danger of the attempt could suggest. Success crowned their effort. Soon they were seen returning deeply laden; but, to lighten the boat, two of their own crew were left behind, whom the small boat afterwards saved. Terrible seas broke over the boat as she crossed the Sound, and filled with fear the hearts of the bystanders on the shore. At length she neared the rocks on her return, when a terrific sea struck her on the stern, buried her in foam, and hurried her with lightning speed upon the rocks. 'They are lost,' was screamed from many in the watching crowd; but a hundred stout hands rushed to the rescue, caught the receding boat, and, amidst the encouraging cheers of the wives, children, and friends of the daring rescuers, they were landed safely. William Fanning, second mate of the Lily, received a compound fracture to a leg which required amputation above the knee and took several months to heal. He stayed in Port St Mary during this time.Early on Tuesday morning 28th December 1852, Mr Enos Lace, grocer and ship broker of Port St Mary, being sub-agent for Lloyds, proceeded with a party of men to the wreck to see would could be saved. They started work on the vessel, but at approximately 8.00 a.m. smoke was observed coming from the middle of the hold. Several carpenters were then employed in cutting a hole in the deck for the purpose of throwing water on the fire to extinguish it. As soon as the air entered the hold spontaneous combustion caused a huge explosion killing all on the isle apart from James Kelly who miraculously survived, albeit with severe facial injuries, despite standing only ten yards from the wreck when the explosion occurred. He recollected nothing of the incident, only finding himself gaining consciousness and sitting on a rock washing himself in his own blood. He later recounted under oath at the inquest that he saw a flash of fire from the deck and saw the head of a companion flying in the air.So violent was the explosion that at the Level Mines, Colby, about three miles off, all the miners in the level 35 fathoms deep, were instantly thrown on their backs, and the lights extinguished. Large and small pieces of timber and other wreckage including human remains were scattered all over the Parish of Rushen as far as Balladoole and even Red Gap just outside of Castletown. Part of a mast or spar was found embedded in a field near the Howe near Port St Mary. Eyewitnesses to the explosion thought that an earthquake had occurred.The following twenty nine salvers were killed, leaving 22 widows and 72 fatherless children: John Fell, age 27, mariner, Port St Mary; William Cowley, age 42, mariner, Port St Mary; William Kermode, age 55, labourer, Port St Mary; Edward Gale, age 42, mariner, Port St Mary; Henry Gale, age 37, mariner, Port St Mary; John Gale, age 45, labourer, Port St Mary; Thomas Witted, age 26, mariner, Port St Mary; John Cubbon, age 57, mariner, Port St Mary; William Lawson, age 52, master mariner, Port St Mary; Thomas Callister, age 43, mariner, Port St Mary; William Taubman, age 42, blockmaker, Port St Mary; John Callister, age 22, mariner, Port St Mary; Samuel Callister, age 29, carpenter; John Callister, age 29, mariner, Port St Mary; Thomas Turnbull, age 32, carpenter, Port St Mary; George Costain, age 32, roper, Port St Mary; William Watterson, age 31, mariner, Port St Mary; Thomas Nelson, age 46, carpenter, Port St Mary; Charles Clugston, age 43, labourer, Port St Mary; Enos Lace, age 51, shopkeeper and roper, Port St Mary; Robert Callister, age 33, baker and mariner, Port St Mary; Edward Qualtrough, age 22, baker, Port St Mary; William Watterson, age 29, mariner, Port St Mary; William Cowin, age 22, mariner, Port St Mary; John Hudgeon, age 21, mariner, Port St Mary; Edward Watterson, age 25, fisherman, Howe; John Watterson, age 31, carpenter, Howe; John Craig, age 32, chief constable, Castletown; and John Wright, age 26, constable, Castletown. 'AWFUL CATASTROPHE in the ISLE OF MAN, caused by the EXPLOSION of 800 Barrels containing 40 Tons of GUNPOWDER, on board the Brig LILY, of Liverpool, wrecked off the Calf of Man, on the 28th December 1852, by which Twenty-nine MEN PERISHED, including the Sub-agent at Lloyd's, and Two Constables. The Inhabitants of Liverpool are respectfully appealed to on behalf of Twenty-two Widows and Seventy-four Orphans, who are left entirely destitute by this calamitous visitation. SUBSCRIPTIONS will be thankfully received by the following Gentlemen, who form the Liverpool Committee: JOHN HOLMES, Esq; JOHN DRINKWATER, Esq; DUNCAN GIBB, Esq; HENRY WINCH, Esq;JAMES McHENRY, Esq;T. T. GLAZEBROOK, Esq; RICHARD STUBBS, Esq; Also by Messrs LEYLAND and BULLINS, Bankers, Treasurers; Mr THOMAS WARBURTON, Exchange Newsroom; Mr JOHN SHIMMIN, 13 Islington; Mr MYLREA, Castle Street; Mr T CORKHILL, Brunswick Road; Mr D RADCLIFFE St James's Street; Mr J LAWSON, at Howard Street; Mr WILLIAM BRIDSON, Bold Street; Mr H K ASPINALL, Birkenhead;The MERCURY OFFICE, Lord Street;The other NEWSPAPER-OFFICES; and by THOMAS ORFORD, Hon Sec, Isle of Man Steam Packet Company, 24, James Street.' In the overwhelming calamity that resulted from the blowing up of the Lily, the gallant conduct of the men who saved her shipwrecked crew on the night before, was apparently lost sight of. The event, however, had not passed unnoticed by the High Bailiff of Douglas, who had influenced a few friends in England to subscribe a small sum of money to distribute amongst the families of the men who had distinguished themselves, in such honorary rewards as he might think advisable. For the purpose of making this distribution a meeting was held at Port St. Mary on the 17th June 1853, at which Edward Moore Gawne, Esq, of Kentraugh, presided. £1 10s was given to each of the small boats crew, and £4 10s each to the widows and only survivor of the larger boats crew, and to each adult and every one of their children was given a Bible strongly bound and with two brass clasps with an account of the disaster inside.On Sunday 22nd October 1854, James Kelly, the only survivor of the Lily disaster, had a piece of wood, one inch long and about half an inch broad, taken out of his neck. His neck and cheek were parts of his body most hurt by the splinters from the explosion. It was feared that there were other pieces still embedded in his neck.During 1899 a man died in America, and before he died, he made a statement, which left little doubt as to the truth of his story. This man, who was a blacksmith, was shoeing a horse when he received a severe kick from the horse, which proved after a few hours, fatal. When he knew that he only had a few hours to live he wished to make a statement which was taken down in writing to the following effect, 'That he belonged to the parish of Rushen in the Isle of Man and that on the morning of 28th December 1852, he along with two others had taken a boat and gone out to the wreck of the Lily before daylight, for the purpose of stealing. They got out all right to the Lily, went on board, and with a lighted candle went below and got what they wanted and proceeded back to the shore again. When about half way in one of them remembered the candle they had left burning, but as the salver's boat was heading out to the wreck, they carried on to shore, when the explosion occurred.' Soon afterwards the man emigrated to America. His two companions also died through accidents.

description:

Event and Historical Information:
The WATER LILY was a wooden schooner built by Pickard at Apledore in 1867. Technical and configuration specifications are given as 135gt, 128nt; 90ft 1in length x 21ft 4in breadth x 11ft 1in depth. At time of loss on 8 November 1892, the vessel was owned by J Helme of Lancaster and registered at that port. The schooner was enroute from Cork to Cardiff when it was run down off Nash Point by the Dublin registered steamship CAPTAIN MCCLURE. The schooner subsequently foundered.

title: Lily Hill Park
description:
Lily Hill Park dates to 1849, and is an example of Victorian emulation of the 18th century English Landscape Park tradition. The park has many exotic pines, specimen trees and ornamental rhododendrons, some of which are early and rare varieties. The park contains a mixture of woodland, species-rich grassland and mire, and includes Starch Copse, an Area of Semi Natural Ancient Woodland. Lily Hill House and its immediate garden are in private ownership. There has been a successful application to the Heritage Lottery Fund to recreate views and vistas, re-instate the footpath system and manage the woodland.

History: Lily Hill House and its grounds were originally developed as a 19th century gentleman's residence in the Jacobean style, built by William Vincent between 1849 and the early 1850s. The Park was developed in phases over the next 30 years.
